audit_question: Is HSConfig still lean enough to maintain with confidence, or is it becoming over-engineered in code size, module boundaries, documentation volume, installed skill maintenance, dependency footprint, and tests?
primary_sources: Command: python -m pytest -q -> 484 passed, 2 skipped in 96.71s (0:01:36)
Command: python scripts\sync_installed_skill.py --check -> HSConfig skill is in sync: C:\Users\darbo\.codex\skills\hsconfig

Command: repository metrics pass over src/tests/docs -> src 55 Python files and 14,833 total lines under src; tests 69 Python files and 36,166 total lines under tests; docs 103 files and 32,958 total lines under docs
Command: tracked docs count -> 98 git-tracked files under docs
Command: internal import fan-in scan -> hsconfig.io imported by 9 modules; hsconfig.source_document_model imported by 8 modules; hsconfig.cli imports 37 internal modules
confirmed_facts: HSConfig still enforces the lean repo boundary at the contract level: pre-run only, no replay parsing, no winrate validation, no candidate promotion, and no post-run tuning.
The runtime dependency footprint is small: pyproject.toml declares one runtime dependency, hearthstone>=9.0.0, plus pytest as the only declared dev dependency.
The installed hsconfig skill is currently synchronized with the repo copy, and the repo contains an explicit sync script plus tests for skill files and sync behavior.
The implementation surface is no longer tiny: src contains 55 Python files, with 53 non-bootstrap modules, about 14.8k total lines, and a mean module size of about 188.9 lines.
Module boundaries are mostly narrow at the low end, with 26 source modules under 100 lines and a median module size of 111 lines.
There is a clear concentration point in hsconfig.cli at 1,057 lines with 34 top-level functions and imports from 37 internal modules, which makes it the main orchestration bottleneck.

Several other modules are materially large for a repo that calls itself lean: operator_summary.py 607 lines, gameplan_contract.py 571, source_document_builder.py 565, guide_claim_builder.py 452, and card_behavior_surface_router.py 423.
The documentation surface is heavy relative to the code surface: docs contains 103 files and about 32.9k lines, with 75 files under docs/research alone and 98 docs files tracked by git.
Test breadth is strong: tests contains 69 Python test files, the suite passed with 484 passed and 2 skipped, and the test tree includes CLI, skill-sync, matrix, multideck, and end-to-end coverage.
The representative proof set is still explicitly bounded to eleven decks: nine core_source_backed_fixture rows and two source_informed_valid_fixture rows, Kingslayer and Boarlock.
strengths: The repo boundary against HSTuner-style sprawl is still explicit in AGENTS.md, README.md, operator docs, the skill file, and tests.
Dependency discipline is very good; there is no sign of a large framework stack or unnecessary package footprint.
The codebase is modular rather than monolithic overall, and many modules remain short enough to reason about locally.
Installed skill maintenance is operationalized instead of manual: there is a dedicated sync script, a documented check flow, and tests that guard drift.
Test confidence is high because the suite is large, passes cleanly, and includes end-to-end and matrix-level regression checks instead of only unit tests.
The eleven-deck matrix provides a concrete cap on scope and a shared proof target, which helps prevent uncontrolled expansion.
gaps_or_risks: The repo is still conceptually lean, but it is no longer small. A 14.8k-line source tree plus a 1,057-line CLI is a real maintainability cost.
The CLI has become the main coupling hub. Its import breadth and function count mean command growth can keep centralizing logic unless orchestration is split further.
Several report and contract modules are large enough that future feature work may increase cognitive load faster than the current naming suggests.

Documentation noise is substantial. Research and audit artifacts now outweigh the implementation surface in tracked volume, which can make the project feel heavier than the runtime product actually is.
Test confidence is strong, but there is no measured line or branch coverage percentage in the current evidence set, so confidence comes from breadth and passing status rather than a coverage budget.
Only two source modules lacked an obvious direct test-name hit in the quick scan, which suggests either indirect coverage or weaker discoverability for those modules.
eleven_deck_implications: The current structure is still good enough to protect the representative eleven-deck proof set, because the docs define that matrix explicitly and the passing suite includes matrix and multideck end-to-end tests.
Nine decks are already treated as core source-backed controls, so the existing architecture is supporting broad pre-game config coverage without obvious collapse.
The two source-informed rows, Kingslayer and Boarlock, show that the repo is using the matrix to expose remaining depth and runtime-surface gaps rather than masking them.
The main risk for the eleven-deck set is not missing tests today; it is that additional orchestration and reporting logic could keep raising the cost of understanding why a matrix row fails.
recommendation: Keep HSConfig scoped as a lean pre-run generator, but start a small maintainability reduction pass instead of adding more workflow surface: first split command orchestration out of hsconfig.cli into narrower command modules or handlers, then freeze or archive low-value research-doc churn so docs/research stops growing faster than the product. Do not widen the representative deck matrix until Kingslayer and Boarlock are closed and the CLI concentration point is reduced.
